blurb: A generic type may refer to itself only uniformly: the self-reference must pass the declaration's own type parameters through unchanged and in order, as `Weird[T]` inside `Weird[T]`. Anything else is polymorphic recursion, such as `Weird[List[T]]` inside `Weird[T]`, or `Pair[B, A]` inside `Pair[A, B]`, and it generates an unbounded set of instantiations, so it is refused at the declaration. The same holds for mutually recursive generics: a partner may be applied only to the declaration's own parameters or to types that mention none, never to a type that wraps one of them.
example:
type Weird[T] = { value: T, next: Option[Weird[List[T]]] }   // ✗ a different instantiation

type Weird[T] = { value: T, next: Option[Weird[T]] }         // ✓ parameters passed through
summary: A generic type refers to itself with arguments other than its own type parameters, in order (`Weird[List[T]]` inside `Weird[T]`, or `Pair[B, A]` inside `Pair[A, B]`), or to a mutually recursive partner with an argument that wraps one of its own parameters (`Inner[List[T]]` inside `Outer[T]`). Such polymorphic recursion generates an unbounded set of instantiations and is refused at the declaration; a self-reference that passes the parameters through unchanged, and a partner applied to the declaration's own parameters or to types that mention none (of any arity), are accepted (#3192).
